title: RBI Expected to Hold Repo Rate at 5.25% as Global Peers Pivot to Hikes
excerpt: Nearly 95% of economists in a Reuters poll predict the central bank will keep rates unchanged when the MPC announces its decision on Wednesday, choosing to look through rising inflation rather than follow peers into tightening.
body:
• The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee began its three-day meeting on August 3 and is expected to hold the repo rate at 5.25% when it announces its decision on August 5.
  • A Reuters poll found 68 of 72 economists expect no change, even as central banks in Europe, Australia, Indonesia, and South Korea have raised rates since the Middle East conflict began.
  • Retail inflation hit 4.38% in June — the first time above the RBI's 4% target in 17 months — but remains within the 2%-6% tolerance band, giving the MPC room to wait.
  • Interest-rate swap markets are pricing roughly 75 basis points of hikes over the next 12 months, signalling traders expect tightening is a matter of when, not if.

The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee began its three-day meeting on Sunday, setting the stage for a closely watched rate decision on Wednesday that will test Governor Sanjay Malhotra's resolve to stand apart from a wave of global monetary tightening.

Nearly 95% of economists polled by Reuters — 68 of 72 — expect the MPC to leave the benchmark repo rate at 5.25%, according to a survey conducted July 21-27. Just four respondents forecast a 25-basis-point hike. The RBI last cut rates in December 2025 and has held steady since then, capping a cycle that delivered a cumulative 125 basis points of easing from February 2025.

A Divergent Path From Global Peers

The expected hold places India on a divergent path from much of the world. Central banks in Europe, Australia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, and South Africa have all raised benchmark borrowing costs since the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began five months ago, driven by surging oil prices and weakening currencies. The Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan, however, have also kept rates on hold.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=zhBzP78b9mE

India's retail inflation accelerated to 4.38% in June, crossing the RBI's 4% target for the first time in 17 months. Yet it remains within the central bank's 2%-6% tolerance band. Core inflation, stripping out volatile food and fuel prices, has stayed contained near 4%.

"Although core and underlying inflation have risen modestly, they remain within the RBI's comfort zone. Consequently, a rate hike is unlikely in 2026 unless core inflation sustains above 4.5%."

— Samiran Chakraborty, Chief India Economist, Citi

Governor Malhotra reinforced this view last week, telling the Hindu BusinessLine that signs of higher fuel prices feeding into more generalised inflation remain limited. He had earlier described talk of rate hikes as "premature."

Rupee Pressure and Capital Inflows

The rupee has fallen nearly 7% against the dollar this year, sliding to a record low ahead of the June MPC meeting. That weakness had fuelled calls for rate hikes to defend the currency, mirroring actions taken by Indonesia and the Philippines.

Instead, the RBI opted for a different playbook. It scrapped capital-gains tax for foreign holders of Indian government bonds, sweetened dollar deposit schemes for non-resident Indians, and launched a $40.8 billion forex swap facility. These measures have drawn roughly $40 billion in foreign inflows, according to Reuters, but the rupee has come under renewed pressure as Gulf hostilities lifted oil prices.

"I do not think the RBI will use interest rate tools to target the rupee because it is ineffective — they cannot simply discard the growth objective, and rate hikes are way more costly now at this particular juncture," said Apoorva Javadekar, chief economist at Muthoot Fincorp.

The Clock Is Ticking on Inflation

Markets, however, are pricing a different trajectory. Interest-rate swap markets have baked in roughly 75 basis points of hikes over the next 12 months, suggesting traders believe tightening is inevitable even if the RBI holds this week.

Wholesale inflation surged to 9.87% in June, and a central bank survey from May showed rising inflation expectations among households. Tanay Dalal, economist at Axis Bank, expects wholesale price pressures to pass through to consumer prices over a three-to-four-month horizon.

"Fundamentally, I think the right call for India is higher rates. They are not going to do it this week but the longer they wait, the more they will be pushed to it."

— Trinh Nguyen, Senior Economist for Emerging Asia, Natixis

Poll medians show inflation averaging 4.8% this fiscal year, up from 4.7% predicted in a May Reuters survey but still below the RBI's own projection of 5.1%. The central bank forecasts GDP growth of 6.6% in FY27, down from 6.9% earlier, with prolonged supply chain disruptions and weather-related shocks posing downside risks.

What to Watch on Wednesday

Even with rates likely on hold, the MPC's language will be scrutinised for signs of a hawkish pivot. Dalal expects the committee to "shift language acknowledging risks of firmer inflation and policy action ahead, while maintaining a data-dependent approach." Kanika Pasricha, chief economic adviser at Union Bank of India, cautioned that if oil prices remain consistently above $90 a barrel, the RBI could consider raising rates in the second half of the fiscal year.

For diaspora investors with exposure to Indian equities, bonds, and NRI deposits, the decision carries direct implications. The RBI's capital-inflow measures — including enhanced NRI deposit schemes — have improved returns for dollar holders, but a potential shift to rate hikes later this year could reshape the calculus for both fixed-income and equity allocations.

The MPC's decision will be announced on Wednesday, August 5.
nri_angle: The RBI's capital-inflow measures and NRI deposit scheme enhancements directly affect diaspora investors, while a potential future rate hike cycle could reshape fixed-income and equity allocations for those with Indian exposure.
